item.book_title: How To Stop Worrying And Start Living

stage_run.summary_md:
## How This Book Was Written—and Why

Dale Carnegie explains the book's origin and methodology. It is not an academic treatise but a practical guide born from a long-running course on 'How to Stop Worrying'. The content is a compilation of tested principles and strategies developed over decades of teaching adults.

## Source of the Material
The book's advice is not the author's invention. It is a distillation of what he has 'learned from others'. For over thirty-five years, Carnegie ran adult-education courses in New York. He observed that a primary concern for his students was worry. In response, he researched and developed a course on the subject, reading everything from ancient philosophers (e.g., Confucius, Buddha, Christ, Marcus Aurelius) to modern psychology texts and conducting hundreds of interviews with people from all walks of life. The book's core is the 'tested rules' that emerged from this course.

## The Book's Practical Nature and Promise
Carnegie positions the book as an action-oriented manual. He promises it will not be a 'dull recital' of ideas but a concrete guide. He makes a specific guarantee: if readers apply its principles, they will have 'less worry in their lives' and will 'start a whole new way of living'. The book is designed to be used, not just read.

stage_run.summary_md:
## Genesis of the Book
Thirty-five years ago, the author quit a sales job he despised to teach adult night classes, freeing his days to write. He chose public speaking as his subject because his college training in it had provided the most practical value, eliminating timidity and giving him courage.

## Teaching at the YMCA
After universities rejected him, he taught at YMCA night schools. Students paid on installment and he was paid a percentage of profits, forcing him to deliver quick, practical results. He was astounded at how quickly students developed self-confidence and secured promotions. Within three seasons, his pay increased from five to thirty dollars a night.

## Research Methodology
He spent seven years preparing: reading philosophers and biographies, interviewing prominent people (e.g., Jack Dempsey, Eleanor Roosevelt), and running a five-year 'laboratory' in his adult classes. Students applied rules on stopping worry and reported results. He listened to thousands of such talks and read hundreds more from prize-winning submissions across over 170 cities.

## Nature of the Book
The book is a practical, documented report, not academic preachment. It names names and gives addresses; it is authentic. It is a collection of successful, time-tested 'recipes'. The author states the content isn't new but is generally not applied; the problem is inaction, not ignorance. The book aims to restate and streamline ancient truths to spur action.
stage_run.first_pass_summary_md:
## Author's Personal Turning Point
Thirty-five years prior, the author was unhappy working a sales job he despised, living in a cockroach-infested room. He decided to quit and teach adult classes at night, freeing his days to write. He chose to teach public speaking because his college training in it had provided the most practical value, wiping out timidity and giving him courage to deal with people.

## Teaching at the YMCA
Universities turned him down. He started teaching at YMCA night schools, where he had to show quick, concrete results because students paid on an installment basis and he was paid a percentage of profits. This forced him to be practical and motivating. He was astounded at how quickly students developed self-confidence and secured promotions. Within three seasons, his pay increased from five to thirty dollars a night.

## Genesis of His Books
From this experience, he wrote *How to Win Friends and Influence People* as a textbook for his classes. Later, he recognized worry as a major problem for his adult students—businesspeople and housewives alike. Searching for a textbook on conquering worry, he found the New York Public Library had only 22 books under 'WORRY' compared to 189 under 'WORMS'.

## Research Methodology for This Book
He spent seven years preparing: reading philosophers and biographies, interviewing prominent people (e.g., Jack Dempsey, Eleanor Roosevelt), and, most importantly, running a five-year 'laboratory' in his adult classes. Students applied rules on stopping worry and reported results. The author listened to thousands of such talks and read hundreds more from prize-winning submissions across over 170 cities.

## Nature of the Book
He describes the book as a practical, fast-moving, documented report, not academic preachment. It names names and gives addresses; it is authentic and vouched for. It is a collection of successful, time-tested 'recipes'. The author states the content isn't new but is generally not applied; the problem is inaction, not ignorance. The book aims to restate and streamline ancient truths to spur action.
